I think you need to be a little sport specific. I'm a middle-distance/long sprinter and my training is very different than how a football player would train; everything I do is in a straight line (I'd probably blow out a knee if I made a hard cut). You, on the other hand, are probably looking to be quick and agile on the field or court.

Try doing 20-40 meter sprints, walk back, and do it again for 20 minutes three times a week. You could also add running patterns. The idea is to go as hard as you can until you start getting sloppy or feel pain. Workouts should total out to around 500 meters to start, and as you get into better shape, increase it to maybe 1000 meters. Remember, you are looking for multiple short bursts of speed, not to run a fast mile, so don't get caught up in running too far (if you ever sprint over 120 meters, ask yourself why). By the way, there's nothing wrong with warming up with a half to one mile run, and the same goes for a cool down.
I have a similar background, this would be a great workout for a soccer mid-fielder. A mid-fielder has to be quick and agile, but they also run a lot, so having endurance is important.

You can achieve your goals; it just takes more effort to get there. In your situation, if you're not incorporating some distance running, you might want to start with that—nothing too intense, perhaps just 3 miles a few times a week. After your run, include some sprint drills. Be cautious with sharp turns; it's important to recognize that you may not be fully conditioned yet, and making aggressive cuts too soon could lead to injury. I worked for a public offering in 2001 and at one point they owed me over 20K in expense reimbursement. It was the same situation; I was told I needed to be somewhere on a Monday (I think it was Thursday) and I told them that as soon as they paid me my money, I'd be glad to go... that issue got resolved quickly, however.

I was sitting on over 1 million in stock options that I couldn't sell for a year (started in June). During this time, they worked me extremely hard, leaving on Mondays at 5:00 am and getting home on Fridays at 11:00 pm—my live-in partner at the time was ready to throw me out. Anyway, I couldn't quit with so much money on the line. Come spring, the stock took a dive, going from over $150 to under $2; at that point, I didn't care much, but I wanted to have a job. Did I mention I had three layers of management above me with no direct reports? This explains why they were working me so hard; I had to support three expensive employees with my labor. 

I had been on the road for over 10 months and was getting tired, and I didn't have an assignment, so I was hoping to be home the upcoming week. As usual, I turned off my phone at 5:00 pm to avoid any unnecessary calls over the weekend (or being sent somewhere). On Monday morning, I turned on my phone, and one of my bosses left me a cheerful message about how I needed to go to a city and get a corporate apartment because I'd be living there for the next 3-6 months. I decided, that's it, I'm done. I called the voicemail boss and got no answer, I called his boss—no answer—and then I called the third-level boss—no answer. Forget it, I guess I'm going into the office today anyway. 

I spent the next hour wiping my computer so I could return it in the same condition I received it. I hopped in the car and drove to the office. The receptionist asked if she could help me; I told her I doubted it and asked for my two lower-level bosses—she mentioned they were out. I said fine, explained that I was an employee, and asked if she had a pair of scissors. She gave me the scissors, and I proceeded to cut up my company credit card in front of her. I then reached into my bag and handed her my laptop and phone. By now, she was a little freaked out and way out of her depth and ran off to find someone. Another manager came rushing down the hall yelling for me to stop. I knew the guy (didn't like him), so I waited. He gave me some nonsense about how important I was to the company and what he needed to do to make me stay—my answer was nothing. I was out the door. Later that day, all three managers called my home phone and asked if they were the reason I left; I told each of them yes, they were.

Here's the strange twist: I quit on Monday, and on Friday, they laid off a third of the company. I have no idea why they would want me to stay.

As long as this is done, nobody usually has a problem; swimmers are used to sharing a lane with many people, and as long as everyone is on the same page, it works fine. The problems happen when the lanes are marked slow to fast, and a slower swimmer hops into the last lane because they don't want to share; it's like driving slowly on a fast track—there is going to be an accident. If you are tapped and you don't get out of the way, you will get tapped again (I personally tickle their feet—really annoying) and again and again. The last step in the process is they will grab your ankles and pull you—sending you backwards and under them—it's aggressive, but you will see it from time to time.
